opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, and I try to be humble about it, because five years ago very few people, including me, would have predicted where we are today.

The way I frame it is through open-endedness. The current paradigm has been extraordinarily successful: train very large models on huge amounts of human-generated data, then fine-tune them. But that data is finite, and a system that only imitates us is bounded by what we've already written down. The really interesting question for the next five years is whether we can build systems that keep generating their own new, interesting, and learnable experiences, and keep improving from them, the way evolution or human science keeps producing novelty without a fixed endpoint.

I think we're going to see much more of that. Foundation models are useful here because they carry a rough notion of what humans find interesting, so you can use them to propose new tasks, critique solutions, and steer exploration in ways that were impossible when we were doing reinforcement learning from scratch in toy environments. Combine that with generative world models, where you can create a practically unlimited range of interactive environments to train agents in, and you get the ingredients for a self-improvement loop that isn't capped by human data.

Concretely, I'd expect agents that run long-horizon, open-ended research projects: forming hypotheses, writing and running experiments, and building on their own findings. I'd expect automated discovery to start contributing meaningfully to science and engineering, not just as a tool that helps a human type faster. And I'd expect embodied agents to get much better as simulation and world models improve.

I want to be careful, though. Open-ended, self-improving systems are by design systems that do things we didn't anticipate. That's the point, and it's also the risk. So I think a big part of the next five years has to be figuring out how to keep these systems understandable and steerable, and how to keep humans meaningfully in the loop. Capability is moving fast, and safety and evaluation have to keep pace with it.

r002.rationale: It describes several expected advances over five years, but does not express the view that anything may be possible for AI in that period.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, and honestly I'm quite careful about making specific predictions, because the field has a habit of humbling anyone who does. But let me try to give you the way I frame it rather than a single answer.

The thing I keep coming back to is open-endedness. For most of the history of machine learning, we've been in a paradigm where humans curate the data, humans define the task, humans decide what counts as progress, and the system optimizes within that box. And that has gotten us remarkably far, large language models are essentially a monument to how far you can get by compressing the collective output of humanity. But there's a ceiling built into it. If the system can only learn from what we've already produced, then in some sense it's bounded by us.

What I think changes over the next five years is that the systems start generating their own learning signal. They propose their own problems, they attempt them, they evaluate the outcomes, and they use that to decide what to try next. We've seen early versions of this in things like AlphaGo's self-play, or in the work on automatically generating environments and curricula, where the agent and the task distribution co-evolve. The missing piece has always been generality: self-play works beautifully in Go because the rules are fixed and verification is free. The question is whether you can get that same flywheel going in domains like mathematics, software, scientific hypothesis generation, where you have at least partial ability to check your own work.

And I think we're seeing the first signs that you can. So if you ask me what AI is capable of in five years, my honest answer is that I expect systems that are not just answering questions but running extended, autonomous processes of discovery. Something that can take a vague research direction, generate a thousand hypotheses, test the ones that are testable in silico, learn from the failures, and come back with a handful that are genuinely novel and genuinely worth a human's attention. That's a very different kind of tool than a chatbot.

The caveat, and it's a big one, is that open-endedness is only valuable if what the system finds is actually interesting and useful to us, and "interesting" is a notoriously slippery thing to specify. A system can be extremely open-ended and extremely good at wandering off into the irrelevant. So a lot of the hard problems in the next five years aren't about raw capability at all. They're about how we steer these processes, how we keep humans meaningfully in the loop when the system is exploring faster than we can follow, and how we make sure the objectives we hand it are the ones we actually meant. I'm optimistic about the capability trajectory. I'm much more cautious about whether we'll have the steering figured out at the same pace.

astra-6.text:
Five years is a very long time in AI, so I’m quite hesitant to make precise predictions. I think we’ll have systems that are much more capable than what we have today, but the interesting question is whether they can go beyond solving tasks that we already know how to specify and start discovering things that genuinely surprise us.

One direction I’m particularly excited about is open-ended learning. Instead of training a model on a fixed dataset for a fixed objective, can we build systems that continually generate new challenges, learn to solve them, and use those capabilities to tackle the next challenge? That could give us a very different trajectory from simply getting better at a particular benchmark.

But there’s a big gap between demonstrating something impressive and having a system that reliably operates over long periods. So I’d look at how well these systems adapt to unfamiliar situations, how they recover from mistakes, and whether they can make sustained progress without us specifying every step. I’m optimistic about that direction, but I wouldn’t pretend we can put a precise date on it.

sol-6.1.text:
Five years is a very long time in AI, so I’m quite hesitant to make precise predictions. I think we’ll see systems that are much more capable, but the question I find particularly interesting is whether they can keep learning and adapting when they encounter something genuinely new. Can they explore, figure out what matters, and acquire skills without us having to specify every task in advance?

If we make progress there, we could have agents that are much more useful across a broad range of problems. But I wouldn’t assume that simply getting better at today’s benchmarks tells us exactly when that will happen. There’s still a lot to understand about generalization and open-ended learning.
